title: Brain Atrophy Analysis in Dementia
summary: A peer-reviewed computer-vision study that converts T1-weighted MRI scans into an interpretable tissue-loss ratio, derives cohort reference bounds, and improves crop-based classification accuracy from 66% to 71% by focusing the analysis on the hippocampal region.
landingDeck: Published in the IEEE ICRITO 2022 proceedings, the research operationalizes visible signs of cerebral atrophy as explicit OpenCV measurements. The resulting pipeline converts color masks into an auditable score, compares that score with reference bounds derived from 2,198 ADNI images, and tests how anatomical focus changes classification performance.
landingHighlights: Analyzes 2,198 ADNI T1-weighted MRI images: 1,172 CDR 0 images and 1,026 images spanning CDR 0.5–2.
Defines the interpretable dem ratio as dark-region density divided by combined white- and grey-region density, connecting every score to visible pixel counts.
Raises reported classification accuracy from 66% with the default crop to 71% with a hippocampal crop, a five-percentage-point improvement.
problem: Manual tracing and segmentation can make brain-atrophy measurement expert-intensive, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce across large MRI collections. The study asks whether visible tissue loss, ventricular expansion, and sulcal widening can be translated into a repeatable image-level score that supports consistent comparison.
approach: The pipeline creates binary masks for black, white, and grey intensity regions; calculates their pixel densities; and computes dem = b / (w + g), where dark space acts as a proxy for cerebrospinal-fluid and open-space patterns and white-plus-grey pixels represent visible tissue. Group means define lower and upper reference bounds, while a controlled crop experiment tests the value of focusing on the hippocampal region.
output: A peer-reviewed five-page IEEE conference paper, a Python/OpenCV measurement method, cohort-derived decision bounds, a three-region interpretation rule, a longitudinal atrophy-rate equation, and a reported crop-based classification improvement from 66% to 71%.

methodology.evaluation: The paper evaluates the method on 2,198 ADNI T1-weighted MRI images divided into 1,172 CDR 0 images and 1,026 CDR 0.5–2 images. It reports dem_low = 0.41, dem_high = 0.83, a worked mildly demented example at dem = 0.60, and accuracy of 66% for the default crop versus 71% for the hippocampal crop.
methodology.boundary: The publication establishes retrospective image-level evidence for the proposed measurement and crop comparison. A clinical validation program would add patient-level cohort design, scanner-diverse external data, diagnostic operating characteristics, and clinical review.

role: I co-authored the paper and built the repeatable Python/OpenCV pipeline that converts MRI intensity regions into quantitative tissue-loss measurements, reference bounds, crop comparisons, and an atrophy-rate method.

pageSections.title: An anatomical hypothesis becomes an explicit, inspectable computer-vision measurement
pageSections.description: The study reduces each T1-weighted MRI image to three visible intensity regions, combines their pixel densities into a tissue-loss ratio, and tests that score against reference bounds derived from 2,198 ADNI images.
pageSections.context: Published in the IEEE ICRITO 2022 proceedings, the paper reports a five-percentage-point accuracy improvement when the analysis is focused on the hippocampal region.

pageSections.title: Make cerebral atrophy measurable without repeated expert tracing
pageSections.description: Dementia can appear in MRI as tissue loss, widened sulci, shrunken gyri, ventricular expansion, and hippocampal change.
pageSections.markdown:
These patterns are clinically meaningful, yet large image collections make repeated manual tracing and segmentation expensive and difficult to standardize. The research therefore narrows a broad diagnostic challenge into a concrete measurement question: can visible tissue and open-space patterns be converted into a repeatable score for comparing MRI images?

The resulting method is deliberately transparent. It uses observable intensity regions, fixed thresholds, binary masks, pixel counts, and a published equation. Every score can be traced back through the calculation to the pixels that produced it, giving researchers an interpretable baseline for studying how anatomical focus and image preparation influence the signal.

pageSections.title: Seven stages connect a labeled scan to an interpretable result

items.label: Group
items.title: Organize images by clinical rating
items.body: Use ADNI T1-weighted MRI images grouped as CDR 0 and CDR 0.5–2 to establish the study cohorts.

items.label: Frame
items.title: Select the anatomical view
items.body: Run the measurement on the default crop and on a hippocampal crop so spatial focus becomes a controlled experimental variable.

items.label: Mask
items.title: Segment three intensity regions
items.body: Create binary masks for black, white, and the defined grey interval using fixed RGB values and ranges.

items.label: Count
items.title: Calculate region densities
items.body: Count selected pixels in each mask and convert those counts into percentages for the analyzed image area.

items.label: Score
items.title: Compute the dem ratio
items.body: Divide dark-region density by the combined white- and grey-region density to quantify open space relative to visible tissue.

items.label: Bound
items.title: Derive group reference values
items.body: Average scores within the labeled cohorts to establish lower and upper bounds for image-level interpretation.

items.label: Compare
items.title: Evaluate crop performance
items.body: Compare default and hippocampal crops through the same scoring workflow and record the classification accuracy of each.

pageSections.title: Three visible image regions produce one auditable atrophy score

items.label: Black · b
items.title: Dark space at RGB [0, 0, 0]
items.body: The numerator represents dark regions associated in the paper with cerebrospinal fluid, sulcal space, and ventricular expansion.

items.label: White · w
items.title: Bright tissue at RGB [255, 255, 255]
items.body: White pixels contribute to the visible-tissue denominator used to contextualize dark area.

items.label: Grey · g
items.title: Mid-range tissue from [70, 70, 70] to [190, 190, 190]
items.body: The thresholded grey interval captures additional visible tissue and joins white pixels in the denominator.

items.label: dem = b / (w + g)
items.title: Open space relative to visible tissue
items.body: A higher ratio indicates more dark area for the measured tissue area and therefore a higher atrophy likelihood under the study model.

pageSections.title: The score keeps the anatomical reasoning and computation connected
pageSections.markdown:
The method treats dark area as a proxy for cerebrospinal-fluid and open-space patterns that increase with ventricular expansion and sulcal widening. White and grey regions represent visible brain tissue. Dividing the first by the second creates a continuous value that can be plotted, averaged across a cohort, compared with reference bounds, or tracked across imaging sessions.

Its simplicity is a technical advantage. A researcher can inspect the crop, review each mask, reproduce the pixel counts, recompute the ratio, and see how a change in framing affects the result. This makes preprocessing part of the scientific question and creates an explainable baseline against which more complex segmentation or learning systems can be compared.

pageSections.title: Cohort averages define three regions of interpretation
pageSections.description: The paper derives a lower bound of 0.41 from the non-demented image group and an upper bound of 0.83 from the dementia image group.

items.label: Below 0.41
items.title: Non-demented region
items.body: Scores below the lower cohort mean are assigned to the paper's non-demented region.

items.title: Intermediate region
items.body: Scores between the reference values represent varying likelihood based on proximity to either bound.

items.label: At or above 0.83
items.title: Dementia region
items.body: Scores reaching the upper cohort mean enter the paper's dementia region.

items.label: Worked example · 0.60
items.title: A result remains visible in context
items.body: The mildly demented example shown in the paper falls inside the intermediate interval, illustrating how the score and bounds are interpreted together.

pageSections.title: Anatomical focus improved reported accuracy from 66% to 71%
pageSections.markdown: The same OpenCV measurement was evaluated with two image framings. The default crop achieved 66% classification accuracy; focusing the analysis on the hippocampal region achieved 71%. The five-percentage-point gain shows that spatial selection materially affects a handcrafted signal and that anatomically informed preprocessing can improve the usefulness of a simple, transparent measurement.

pageSections.title: The same score supports measurement of change across imaging sessions
pageSections.markdown:
The paper extends the image-level score with an atrophy-rate equation: subtract the initial dem value from the final dem value and divide by the time interval. This turns the static measurement into a method for comparing repeated MRI observations using a common unit.

That extension matters because dementia is progressive. A continuous, reproducible score creates a practical bridge from cross-sectional image analysis to future longitudinal studies that can ask how quickly structural change is occurring and how the rate differs across cohorts or interventions.

pageSections.title: A peer-reviewed retrospective image-level measurement and crop study
pageSections.markdown:
The paper establishes the method on 2,198 labeled ADNI MRI images and reports the score bounds, worked example, and default-versus-hippocampal crop result. The reported unit is images, and the published accuracy comparison is crop-based.

A clinical validation program would extend the research with patient-level cohort design, scanner-diverse external data, sensitivity and specificity, calibration, prospective evaluation, and clinical review. The separate four-class TensorFlow notebook is documented on its own page so each study retains a clear method and evidence record.
